title: Chenchen (Sabrina) Peng
text:
Working Papers
Offshoring and Knowledge Spillovers (Job Market Paper) [PDF]
Abstract
When U.S. manufacturers offshore to China, their affiliates and suppliers obtain the knowledge required to produce the goods. Did that knowledge then diffuse to nearby producers, strengthening the Chinese companies that export to the United States? Linking firm-level production records to transaction-level imports data from the U.S. Census Bureau, I measure offshoring by all 1997 U.S. manufacturers and estimate the knowledge spillovers from offshoring. A staggered difference-in-differences design shows that exports to the U.S. by Chinese producers that never receive offshoring orders rise 16 percent two to five years after the first offshoring order in their city and industry, relative to city–industries not yet reached by offshoring. In a trade model with knowledge diffusion, offshoring firms do not internalize that these spillovers lower U.S. aggregate price index but erode other U.S. firms' profits; whether they offshore too much or too little is theoretically ambiguous. A per-firm tax or subsidy on offshoring, scaled to the size of the spillovers, corrects the externality, while protection of trade secrets removes the externality without changing the level of offshoring.
Workforce Age Structure and Frontier Technology Adoption: Evidence from Newly Released Software [PDF]
with Tra Nguyen
Abstract
This paper provides causal evidence that aging slows technology adoption and sheds light on why. Using Lightcast job postings, we track local adoption of 15 software technologies following their releases, instrumenting local age composition with a Bartik-style measure based on historical age structure and national survival rates. Employers in older labor markets post increasingly fewer vacancies requiring the newest software: at year 4, a one-standard-deviation increase in the older-worker share reduces new-technology postings by about 15% of pre-release legacy postings share. The gap is also larger for more difficult technologies, which we measure using new LLM-based difficulty indices. We then develop a model to separate three potential channels through which aging affects technology adoption: shorter work horizon, legacy technology experience loss, and reduced learning efficiency. Removing experience loss reduces the age adoption gap by about 88%, more than removing differences in horizons or learning efficiency. The model also shows that policies affecting workforce age structure have different implications for adoption. Relative to replacement-level fertility with retirement at 70, and assuming zero net migration, a total fertility rate of 1.6 lowers aggregate adoption by 7.5%, whereas raising the retirement age to 75 has almost no effect.
